## Abstract

Understanding how food web structure varies across broad spatial gradients is essential for identifying general principles of ecosystem organization and resilience under global change. We analyzed seven highly resolved marine food webs spanning a latitudinal gradient from 48°S to 78°S in the Southwest Atlantic and Antarctic region to evaluate how ecosystem area, latitude, human impact, and number of trophic species are associated with network structure and dynamic stability. We quantified connectance, link density, mean trophic level, modularity, SVD complexity, rank deficiency, and dynamic stability, and related each metric to the four predictors using site-level Bayesian regressions that incorporate the uncertainty derived from a metaweb assembly model as a measurement-error term. Because the dataset comprises only seven independent food webs, we assessed the robustness of each relationship by refitting the models with each food web excluded in turn.

Ecosystem area showed the most consistent associations: larger ecosystems had higher mean trophic level, link density, connectance, and SVD complexity, and these associations held in all seven exclusions. The number of trophic species was positively associated with rank deficiency and modularity and negatively with connectance, but these associations lost support when a single food web, Burdwood Bank, was excluded. Latitude was positively associated with link density and SVD complexity, although these associations depended on three of the seven food webs, and its associations with connectance and trophic level did not survive exclusion. Human impact showed no clear association with any metric, possibly because the cumulative impact index integrates stressors whose effects on food web structure differ in magnitude and direction.

Among the predictors considered, ecosystem area showed the most consistent associations with marine food web structure in the Southwest Atlantic and Antarctic. Patterns associated with species richness and latitude should be treated as exploratory and require evaluation with additional independent food webs.

## Introduction

Understanding how ecological network structure varies across broad spatial gradients can reveal general principles of ecosystem organization and how anthropogenic drivers shape ecosystem functioning [@Tylianakis2017; @Kortsch2019]. In marine systems, food webs integrate multiple ecological processes and functions such as species interactions, energy transfer, and functional organization that collectively determine ecosystem resilience and stability under environmental change. As a result, trophic interaction networks provide a powerful framework for evaluating ecosystem responses to both natural environmental gradients and human‐induced stressors [@Bascompte2009].

Marine food webs across the Southern Hemisphere are exposed to distinct, but often overlapping stressors, including fishing pressure, ocean warming, biological invasions, sea ice decline, and glacial retreat, each expected to leave characteristic signatures on food web structure and stability [@Queiros2024]. A recent review covering the Southwest Atlantic and Antarctic regions synthesized evidence linking dominant regional stressors to potential changes in food-web connectance, modularity, stability, energy fluxes, and functional diversity [@Marina2024b]. The review identified different dominant stressors among areas, mainly warming but alien species and fisheries in the Beagle Channel and Burdwood Bank, and formulated area-specific hypotheses on how they may affect food web properties, suggesting that responses may differ among ecosystems along the gradient. Beyond stressors, we expect differences in ecosystem size among food webs to contribute to variation in food web structure across latitude, such as in food chain length.

According to the ecosystem size hypothesis, larger ecosystems are expected to sustain longer food chains due to higher species richness, greater habitat heterogeneity, and increased persistence of higher trophic levels [@Post2000; @Post2007]. Empirical support for this pattern has been reported for both freshwater and marine systems [@Takimoto2008]. However, ecosystem size alone does not determine food chain length; community composition and energetic constraints also matter [@Post2002]. For example, large-bodied herbivorous or omnivorous consumers may provide relatively short pathways of energy transfer from primary producers to top predators, reducing mean food chain length [@Arim2016; @Jardine2016]. Thus, large or highly productive ecosystems do not necessarily support longer food chains. Consistent with this view, studies of marine food webs have found no universal latitudinal pattern in food chain length or maximum trophic level, suggesting that biogeographic gradients interact with community composition and energetic constraints rather than acting as simple drivers [@JakeVanderZanden2007].

Another key dimension shaping food web structure along spatial gradients is human-driven impact [@Kraufvelin2026]. Anthropogenic pressures are often hypothesized to erode network organization and drive food webs toward more random and simpler structures, potentially reducing ecological complexity and stability [@Kraufvelin2026; @Mestre2022]. However, empirical patterns depend strongly on ecosystem type. At a global scale, regions with higher disturbance tend to exhibit more random network structures, whereas less disturbed systems show a greater prevalence of scale-free organization. Notably, marine food webs appear to deviate from this general pattern, exhibiting a shift toward more scale-free structures with increasing human impact [@Mestre2022]. Empirical evidence from marine systems therefore remains mixed, with reported changes in connectance and energy pathways varying across ecosystems and spatial contexts [@Mestre2022]. In parallel, recent global syntheses indicate that connectance in marine food webs tends to increase toward higher latitudes, although this pattern is partly confounded by variation in species richness and by differences between coastal and oceanic systems [@Albouy2019].

Environmental conditions and anthropogenic pressures can influence food web structure and stability, potentially favoring network configurations that buffer the effects of perturbations [@Borrelli2015; @Monteiro2017]. Network modularity represents an important structural property linking food web organization to stability. Modularity is assumed to buffer ecosystems against perturbations by limiting the spread of disturbances between modules across the network [@Thebault2010]. Consequently, modularity may vary systematically along environmental gradients [@Kortsch2019], or in response to climate change and human activities, reflecting emergent adaptive responses of local food web organization to disturbance regimes.

To test these hypotheses, we adopt a macroecological approach, examining how marine food web complexity, structure, and stability relate to ecosystem area, latitude, human impact, and the number of trophic species. This approach contributes to ongoing efforts to identify general mechanisms governing ecological network organization across spatial scales and environmental contexts [@Cirtwill2015; @Welti2015; @Kortsch2021; @Frelat2022; @Jordan2024]. We relate each food web metric to these four predictors across food webs spanning the Southwest Atlantic–Antarctic latitudinal gradient and assess the robustness of the relationships by excluding individual food webs in turn. This provides a conservative assessment of the associations between these predictors and marine food web organization across contrasting ecological and anthropogenic contexts.

## Methods

### Food web data and standardization

All the food webs considered in the present study have been previously described in individual peer-reviewed publications [San Jorge Gulf in @Funes2022; Beagle Channel in @Rodriguez2022; Burdwood Bank in @Marina2024a; North and South Scotia Sea in @Lopez-Lopez2022; Potter Cove in @Marina2018; Weddell Sea in @Jacob2011]; for a comprehensive overview see also [@Marina2024b]. The food webs span a latitudinal gradient from the San Jorge Gulf (48°S) to the Weddell Sea (78°S), covering a range of ecosystem types, including coastal bays, continental shelf areas, and open-ocean systems (Figure 1). 
Although these food webs were constructed using a similar methodology [@Gauzens2013], we identified dissimilarities in the trophic resolution of several functional groups (e.g., phytoplankton, zooplankton, marine mammals, and seabirds). To minimize this trophic disparity among datasets, we modified the food webs in the following way:
For the Beagle Channel, North and South Scotia Sea, we increased the resolution of high-trophic levels, that is, we added marine mammals and seabirds as well as their diets.
For the North and South Scotia Sea and the Weddell Sea, we reduced the resolution of basal species mainly by collapsing the community diversity of phytoplankton into functional groups (e.g., Bacillariophyceae, Chrysophyceae, Dinophyceae). By applying the same criteria to all food webs, these adjustments brought the resolution of top predators (marine mammals and seabirds) and of basal species (phytoplankton functional groups) to a comparable level across networks while preserving their key ecological structure, enabling robust cross-site comparisons along the latitudinal gradient. With this, we aim to tackle issues with food web resolution when comparing food web structures compiled by different researchers [@Brimacombe2025]. Details on the standardization process are available in the Supplementary Material.

### Human Impact Index

To quantify anthropogenic pressure on marine ecosystems, including climate-driven stressors, we used the most recent version of the cumulative human impact index developed by @Halpern2025, which has been widely applied in marine ecological and network-based studies [@Mestre2022; @Foley2015]. This index integrates spatially explicit data on multiple human pressures acting on marine ecosystems, combining both current conditions and projected impacts.

The updated framework incorporates ten anthropogenic pressures grouped into five major categories: climate (water temperature, air–heat index, sea-level rise), ocean chemistry (ocean acidification and dissolved oxygen), land-based pressures (nutrient inputs, light pollution, and coastal human population density), net primary productivity, and fisheries (biomass removal). Pressure layers are mapped globally at 10-km spatial resolution and combined with habitat-specific vulnerability weights to estimate cumulative impacts on marine habitats [@Halpern2025].

In this study, we used cumulative impact estimates corresponding to present-day conditions (~2010–2020), consistent with the temporal coverage of the food webs analyzed. Impact values represent the average cumulative pressure experienced by marine habitats within each spatial unit, with values $\ge 1$ indicating conditions under which habitats are unlikely to persist in their current state. For each food web, we calculated the mean cumulative human impact index across the spatial extent of the corresponding network and used this value as a continuous predictor in subsequent analyses.

### Estimating variability of metrics using a metaweb model

We assumed that the compiled and standardized food webs represent the full set of potential trophic interactions for each system. Because species may be absent from a given site at particular times, not all potential interactions are necessarily realized, and the local number of species and links may fluctuate through time. To capture this variability, we used a metaweb assembly model [@Saravia2022], treating each compiled food web as the metaweb corresponding to its respective area. Such a modeling framework helps unite local ecological interactions and broader biogeographic patterns and processes [@Mestre2026].

In this model, species colonize a local site from the metaweb with probability $c$ and go locally extinct with probability $e$, following the logic of island biogeography theory [@MacArthur1967] while explicitly incorporating food web structure. Colonizing species arrive with their full set of potential trophic interactions, but only interactions involving species present in the local community are realized. Non-basal species are subject to secondary extinction with probability $se$ when none of their prey are present. Local extinctions may therefore propagate through the network via cascades of secondary extinctions, modulated by $se$.

The three model parameters ($c$, $e$, and $se$) were estimated separately for each compiled food web using approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) [@Beaumont2010]. We used the package `abc` with the rejection algorithm [@Csillery2012]. Model fit was evaluated using the Euclidean distance between the simulated values of species richness and connectance and the observed values of the same compiled food web that served as the metaweb. Prior distributions were uniform: $c \sim U(0.01, 0.3)$, $e \sim U(0.001, 0.5)$, and $se \sim U(0.1, 0.9)$. For each web, we ran 10,000 simulations and retained as accepted parameter sets those of the 5% of simulations with the smallest distance. The model was implemented in R using the package `meweasmo` [@Saravia2022b].

To assess whether the metaweb assembly model adequately captures the structural properties of compiled food webs, we compared observed network metrics with the distributions obtained from simulated networks. Across all metrics considered--link density, connectance, complexity (SVD), rank deficiency, mean trophic level, and modularity--observed values consistently fell within the range of variation generated by the model (Figures S3–S5), with the exception that link density in compiled networks tended to exceed the simulated distribution, as expected when not all species co-occur simultaneously in simulated networks. This agreement indicates that the metaweb assembly framework reproduces realistic levels of network organization, supporting its use for quantifying variability and uncertainty in food web structure. Unlike the other network metrics considered in this study, dynamic stability already incorporates uncertainty through randomizations of interaction strengths. Therefore, additional variability derived from the metaweb assembly model was not estimated for this metric. For each food web, the site-level mean and standard deviation of every metric across the retained metaweb-derived replicates were used as the point estimate and associated uncertainty in the site-level regression models described below (see Statistical analyses).

### Network metrics

We described the food web complexity, structure and stability using commonly-used and relatively novel metrics in ecological network studies [@Delmas2018; @Landi2018; @Montoya2006]. For each metric, Table 1 gives its definition, its ecological meaning in a binary food web, and the response expected to the predictors analyzed. Details on the methodology to calculate the novel metrics, such as SVD complexity, rank deficiency and dynamic stability, can be found in Supplementary Methods.

#### Statistical analyses

We related each network metric to ecosystem area (log-transformed), latitude, mean human impact index, and number of trophic species ($S$) using a separate Bayesian regression for each metric. For each food web, we summarized the distribution of each metric across its retained metaweb-derived replicates by the replicate mean and standard deviation, after applying the transformations described below, so that simulated replicates were not treated as independent observations.

Proportion metrics (C, Modularity, Rank Deficiency) were logit‐transformed, strictly positive variables (Link Density and dynamic stability) were log‐transformed, and SVD complexity and mean trophic level were standardized (z‐scores). Dynamic stability was quantified as $\log(-\lambda_{\max})$, using the eigenvalue with the maximum real part of the community matrix, multiplied by -1 so that larger values indicate a stronger tendency to return to equilibrium.

Each regression included a measurement-error term that incorporates the site-level standard deviation derived from the metaweb-based replicates directly into the likelihood, together with an additional residual variance component. Each model therefore uses seven site-level observations, one per food web, to estimate four slopes (area in km^2^, log-transformed), an intercept and a residual standard deviation, and propagates the uncertainty associated with metaweb-based replication into the estimated relationships. All predictors were centered and scaled prior to analysis, and we used weakly informative priors on the slopes and the residual standard deviation to regularize the estimates (Supplementary Methods). With this sample size the posterior distributions retain substantial uncertainty and can depend on individual food webs, so we interpret the estimated slopes as exploratory associations rather than as evidence of general or causal effects.

Collinearity among predictors was assessed with variance inflation factors (VIF) [@Zuur2010]. Because all models share the same predictors and food webs, a single set of VIFs applies to every metric. VIFs ranged from 1.68 (human impact) to 3.10 (number of trophic species) (Table S3); only the latter slightly exceeded the conservative threshold of 3 proposed by @Zuur2010.

All models were fit with four chains of 4,000 iterations (2,000 warmup) using `brms` with the `CmdStan` backend, and convergence was assessed with R-hat and effective sample size diagnostics (all $\hat{R} \leq 1.005$, no divergent transitions; Table S4). Support for each predictor–response relationship was summarized as the posterior probability of a consistent sign, calculated as the maximum of the posterior probabilities that the slope was positive or negative; we discuss effects for which this probability exceeded 0.90.

Given the small sample size (n = 7), an apparent relationship reaching this threshold under the full dataset can nonetheless be driven by one or two highly influential food webs. We therefore assessed the robustness of every relationship meeting this threshold with a leave-one-site-out procedure: each of the seven models was refit seven times, excluding one food web at a time, and we recorded whether the direction and posterior support ($\geq$ 0.90) of the corresponding effect were preserved. We classify an effect as robust when this was the case in at least four of the seven leave-one-site-out refits (i.e., it failed to hold in no more than three exclusions); effects that failed to hold in four or more refits are reported but interpreted with substantial caution, as they may reflect the influence of one or two food webs rather than a general pattern.

All data transformations, model specifications, priors, and code required to reproduce the analyses, including the site-level restructuring and leave-one-site-out diagnostics described above, are provided in the Supplementary Materials and in a public GitHub repository (https://github.com/EcoComplex/SouthMetawebs), with archived code and data available on Zenodo (doi: xxxxxxxx).

## Results

Across the seven food webs analyzed, network metrics varied markedly in magnitude and variability (Table S1). Connectance (C) and link density (LD) spanned an order of magnitude, with the highest values observed in both Scotia Sea networks and the lowest in Burdwood Bank. Mean trophic level (TL) ranged between 2.2 and 3.5, whereas SVD complexity showed moderate variation among systems. Rank deficiency, reflecting the effective dimensionality of interaction matrices, varied substantially across food webs, with the highest values observed in Burdwood Bank and the Weddell Sea. Modularity also showed a broad range among networks, indicating differing degrees of compartmentalization. Dynamic stability, quantified by the maximum eigenvalue of the community matrix, also differed among systems, with Scotia Sea networks tending to exhibit more negative eigenvalues than lower-latitude food webs, consistent with faster return rates to equilibrium following perturbations.

Site-level Bayesian regressions (n = 7 independent food webs per model; see Methods) identified ecosystem area as the predictor with the strongest and most consistent associations with food web structure among the 28 metric–predictor combinations examined (Figure 2). Eleven combinations reached the 0.90 posterior support threshold under the full dataset, and nine of them met the leave-one-site-out robustness criterion (Table S2).

Curves span the central 99% of each posterior distribution, the inner shaded area marks the central 80% interval (which excludes zero exactly when the posterior probability of a consistent sign exceeds 0.90), and the vertical line within each curve marks the posterior median. Background shading marks relationships that reached the 0.90 posterior support threshold and met the leave-one-site-out robustness criterion (blue: positive; red: negative); unshaded relationships either did not reach this threshold or did not meet the criterion (Table S2).](Figures/Bayesian_post_slopes.png)

Log-transformed area was positively associated with mean trophic level (posterior probability of a consistent positive sign, p = 0.991), SVD complexity (p = 0.983), link density (p = 0.982), and connectance (p = 0.965) (Figure 3). All four associations kept the same sign and remained above the 0.90 support threshold in each of the seven leave-one-site-out refits (Table S2).

Solid black lines show posterior mean predictions from the site-level Bayesian regressions with the other three predictors held at their mean, back-transformed to each metric's original scale; shaded areas indicate 95% credible intervals. Points are partial residuals: the observed mean of each food web after removing the estimated contribution of the other three predictors, with vertical bars showing the 95% quantiles of the metaweb-derived replicates shifted by the same amount. Area is shown in km^2^ on a logarithmic scale; the models used standardized log-transformed area.](Figures/Bayesian_TL_SVDC_LD_vs_Area_partial_origscale.png)

The number of trophic species (S) was positively associated with rank deficiency (p = 0.960) and modularity (p = 0.954), and negatively associated with connectance (p = 0.934). The first two associations fell below the support threshold in only one refit, when Burdwood Bank was excluded; the association with connectance failed in three refits, when Burdwood Bank (where the slope reversed sign), San Jorge Gulf, or Beagle Channel were excluded. Latitude was positively associated with SVD complexity (p = 0.955) and link density (p = 0.940); both associations failed in three refits, when Burdwood Bank, San Jorge Gulf, or the Weddell Sea were excluded. Positive associations of latitude with connectance (p = 0.934) and mean trophic level (p = 0.914) failed in five of the seven refits and did not meet the robustness criterion (Table S2). Area was not associated with modularity (p = 0.812), and the associations of area, latitude and S with dynamic stability did not reach the 0.90 support threshold (p = 0.720, 0.711, and 0.663, respectively).

Effects of human impact were comparatively weak and uncertain, with no predictor–response combination reaching the 0.90 support threshold (maximum p = 0.866, for SVD complexity).

## Discussion

Ecosystem area showed the most consistent associations with food web structure and complexity among the predictors examined, with larger ecosystems supporting higher trophic levels, greater interaction density, and higher structural complexity (SVD complexity). These associations held in every leave-one-site-out refit, so they do not depend on any single food web in our dataset. Such patterns are consistent with theoretical expectations that larger ecosystems can sustain more complex food webs through greater spatial extent, increased habitat availability, and enhanced persistence of higher trophic levels [@Galiana2018; @Gravel2011; @Takimoto2013]. Higher trophic levels in larger ecosystems are also consistent with greater vertical diversity, which in a global analysis of 318 food webs underlay the positive effects of biodiversity on ecosystem functioning [@Barnes2026a]. Food webs from larger ecosystems also exhibited higher link density, indicating broader average diets and more alternative trophic pathways, which may sustain ecosystem functioning and buffer perturbations by providing alternative routes of energy transfer when particular interactions are disrupted [@Biggs2020; @Sanders2018]. Given the consistency of this pattern relative to the other relationships considered here, we regard ecosystem area as the predictor most consistently associated with marine food web organization in this study.

The number of trophic species was positively associated with rank deficiency and modularity and negatively associated with connectance. The negative association with connectance agrees with the expected trade-off between species richness and connectance, whereby the number of realized interactions increases more slowly than the number of possible interactions as species accumulate [@Dunne2002; @Vermaat2009]. The positive association with rank deficiency indicates that species-rich food webs contain more species with redundant interaction profiles, consistent with additional species repeating existing trophic roles rather than adding new ones [@Strydom2021]. However, all three associations lost support when Burdwood Bank was excluded. This food web had the lowest connectance and link density, the highest modularity, and the second highest rank deficiency in our dataset (Table S1), so these associations rely strongly on a single system and should be regarded as exploratory until they can be evaluated with additional food webs spanning a broader range of species richness.

Latitude was positively associated with link density and SVD complexity, but these associations met the robustness criterion only at its limit, losing support when Burdwood Bank, San Jorge Gulf, or the Weddell Sea were excluded, the latter two located at the ends of the gradient. The positive associations of latitude with connectance and mean trophic level did not meet the criterion. Thus, the previously reported increase in marine food web connectance toward higher latitudes [@Albouy2019] was not consistently supported by our analyses, and the absence of a robust latitudinal pattern in mean trophic level agrees with the lack of a universal latitudinal trend in food chain length [@JakeVanderZanden2007]. With food webs at only seven positions along the gradient, these latitudinal patterns should be regarded as exploratory and evaluated using additional food webs spanning a broader range of latitudes.

Given the widely accepted view that modularity can enhance food web stability by limiting the propagation of perturbations [@Eskuche-Keith2023], we initially expected a positive relationship between modularity and the human impact index. However, no such relationship was detected, either under the full dataset or in the site-level analysis reported here. One possible explanation is that human pressures may simultaneously promote and erode modularity through opposing mechanisms. While disturbance can favor compartmentalization by isolating impacts, chronic anthropogenic stressors often homogenize ecosystems by selectively removing sensitive species and interactions, thereby reducing network compartmentalization. This interpretation is consistent with the findings of @Mestre2022, who showed that fishing pressure can erode modular structure in marine food webs. The combined action of these opposing processes could result in a net neutral relationship between modularity and overall human impact in our analysis. Moreover, the composite nature of the human impact index may mask contrasting effects of its individual components on modularity and other network metrics. Disentangling these component‐specific effects represents an important avenue for future research.

Beyond the limitations of the composite human impact index, another constraint on detecting anthropogenic effects stems from the nature of the food web data themselves. The networks analyzed here capture the topology of trophic interactions (the presence or absence of links between species) but not the frequency, intensity, or proportional contribution of them. Anthropogenic stressors such as fisheries, pollution, or climate change may alter the strength of trophic links or shift diet composition without adding or removing the links themselves. For example, in the San Jorge Gulf, there is evidence that several fish species have shifted their diets over recent decades [@Belleggia2019, @Pasti2024], yet for most species, no updated dietary information has been available since 2000 [@Rincon-Diaz2024]. As long as a trophic interaction persists between species, even if its quantitative importance changes substantially, such reorganization remains invisible in a binary adjacency matrix. In this sense, binary food web topology is relatively insensitive to the kind of gradual reorganization mediated by interaction strength that anthropogenic stressors typically drive. Moreover, the dietary information underlying these networks was compiled from studies spanning several decades, with data for different species collected across different periods, locations, and ecological contexts. This temporal heterogeneity means that the networks represent a time-averaged, composite snapshot of trophic structure rather than a record tied to any specific period, even if the human impact index was computed for present-day conditions (2010–2020). Resolving these limitations would require quantitatively weighted food webs in which interaction strengths and/or diets are restricted to a particular period. The construction of weighted food webs with most interactions restricted to a particular period would be important for future efforts to use food web structure as an indicator of anthropogenic impact in marine ecosystems.

Modularity and dynamic stability are often hypothesized to trade off against one another because they capture different dimensions of a food web's response to perturbation: resistance to the spread of disturbance versus the rate of return to equilibrium [@Donohue2016; @Thebault2010; @Carpentier2021]. Our data do not allow this trade-off to be evaluated: modularity was associated only with the number of trophic species, and that association depended on a single food web, while no predictor reached the support threshold for dynamic stability. We note the hypothesized trade-off here as motivated by prior theoretical and empirical work rather than as a finding of the present analysis, and see it as a candidate pattern worth revisiting once a larger set of independent food webs becomes available.

To determine whether the relationships identified here represent general features of marine food webs or patterns specific to the Southwest Atlantic-Antarctic region, additional highly resolved food webs from other marine basins will be needed, a limitation made explicit by the leave-one-site-out diagnostics applied throughout this study, which showed that several relationships depended on one or a few food webs. At present, marine food web research remains geographically imbalanced, with a disproportionate focus on Northern Hemisphere ecosystems [@Xu2024; @Poisot2021]. Expanding the availability of comparable food web datasets from the Southern Hemisphere will be essential both for evaluating the generality of the patterns detected here and for supporting more complex multivariate models than the seven independent food webs currently available can reliably identify.

By incorporating metaweb-derived uncertainty at the food web level and conducting leave-one-site-out sensitivity analyses, we provide a cautious assessment of associations between environmental and spatial predictors and marine food web structure and stability. Ecosystem area showed the most consistent associations among the predictors examined, with larger ecosystems tending to have higher trophic levels, greater interaction density, and higher structural complexity, and these associations held regardless of which food web was excluded. Associations involving species richness and latitude depended on one to three food webs, and those of latitude with connectance and trophic level did not survive exclusion. These patterns remain tentative and require evaluation using a larger, more geographically representative set of independent food webs.

More broadly, this study highlights the importance of sensitivity analyses in macroecological syntheses based on few independent food webs. Even a conservative posterior support threshold cannot establish a general relationship when individual observations strongly influence the estimates. Although limited by the small sample of seven food webs, leave-one-site-out analyses help distinguish relationships that remain consistent across exclusions (e.g. between area and food web structure) from those that depend on particular systems. We recommend similar checks to support cautious interpretation of other macroecological syntheses based on small compiled datasets.
